claims.text: The multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy initially has an intact protective high-temperature oxide layer.
Mechanical wear disrupts or removes the protective oxide film at elevated temperature.
Removal of the oxide film exposes chemically heterogeneous and less corrosion-resistant internal surfaces.
The exposed dissimilar phases have different corrosion potentials.
Potential differences between exposed phases produce localized micro-galvanic cells.
Localized corrosion undermines surface structural integrity and increases susceptibility to wear.
Wear-induced oxide disruption and corrosion-induced surface weakening form a positive feedback loop.
The positive feedback between wear and corrosion causes synergistic overall degradation.
Simultaneous wear and corrosion will produce greater total material loss than the sum of wear-only and corrosion-only losses.
Simultaneous exposure will produce deeper localized corrosion attack than isolated corrosion.
Simultaneous exposure will produce deeper or thicker wear tracks than isolated wear.
The proposed mechanism requires an initially stable oxide film.
The proposed mechanism requires a multiphase microstructure containing regions with different electrochemical potentials.
Wear must be sufficient to remove the oxide scale but insufficient to cause corrosion-independent mechanical failure.
The magnitude of wear-corrosion synergy depends on microstructure, corrosive-environment aggressiveness, and wear rate.

contradictions.description: The mechanism states that mechanical wear removes the protective oxide film, whereas the baseline describes a wear-only condition in which the oxide layer remains intact. Without specifying a lower-severity wear control or another means of preserving the film, these statements conflict.
